en: Where is this Ten-Powered One, unspotted by defects, whose mastery of conduct is all-pervading; and where is this mind of mine, sluggish from turning within the rutting-trough of worldly existence?
Yet, because the dust cast at you becomes fruitful through its offering, my speech assumes a vocal quality by following after praise. (Śārdūlavikrīḍita)

The unique virtues of those who have transcended the objects of the mind and possess the vision of tranquility do not fall within the range of speech, for they are too subtle for those like me; yet they reach it in part.
For the jewels of the ocean appear to seekers on the sandy shores near the water, while who could grasp the moonlight from the inner glow of the waves? Js_2 //

O Blessed One, that stream of yours—which was energetic in deeds following the path to awakening for the great ones, and which flowed with the compassion of the Victors for the arising of the world’s welfare—purifies even those whose stains have been removed by the expansion of the enjoyment of the knowable when it is now being proclaimed; how much more so, then, do your virtues [purify] those who are already set toward awakening? Js_3 //

Because you directed your thoughts toward awakening—remaining unshaken even after observing the forward-rushing behavior of the wild elephant of passion—you have become, as it were, the vessel upon which the immortals from heaven long place the glory of the consecration of Dharma; thus they created an offering of flowers that reached to the tips of your unshaken hair.

Seeing a tigress dwelling within the depths of a mountain cave, her belly exhausted by the pain of hunger and driven by a singular urgency to devour her cubs, you—your mind permeated with compassion—cast off your own body, clad in bark garments and bearing matted hair; by that act, you became the refuge for embodied beings who turn away from the clefts of the mountain of worldly existence.
When you, assuming the form of an elephant as white as a mountain of snow and sugar, moved toward the great rocky peak to destroy the calamities of the embodied beings dwelling within the forest,
I believe that by your hurling yourself against its slopes, the utterly dark activities of the envious were utterly shattered.

When you were Candraprabha, with a body like the moon that illuminates the world’s sky, you gave to a supplicant brahmin the crest-jewel from your head—its hair black at the tips—with its luster shining;
it was severed like a lotus plucked by a sword, its root cut away. By that act, you have become the preceptor of these worlds, like an *uṣṇīṣa* upon their heads.

O Jina, because you gave away to a petitioner your young sons— whose bodies were as tender as young lotuses— and your wives, who followed you with devotion, their eyes cast down and bearing their swaying topknots, the faces of the daughters of Māra surely became slow with shame, their petal-like eyelashes drooping in contraction.

O Lord, because you were formerly a bird dwelling in forest lands who contemplated beds and dreams, you shattered all worldly attachments and proclaimed the path of the Supreme while the world remained unimpaired; by that Kapiñjala vow which you, the observer of vows, expanded to its full extent, may your feet become the refuge for those whose crowns provide shade against the disease of ignorance.

O Lord, because you formerly sustained the moon—who subsisted on leaves, water, and fruit—and out of a long-standing habit of compassion offered hospitality to that guest for the duration of its stay, even now the mark upon the lunar disc is seen as a rabbit upon the earth; it is actually your own fame, O Moon, that has ascended into the fire of blazing sparks.

I believe that the Earth, fearing every limb of yours might be shattered by the flashing sword of the God of Love—who, with eyes red with anger, drew a frown between his brows—was unable to bear parting from you for even a moment, her mind unshaken; therefore, the unrestrained arrows of Smara must have met with a breakage at their very feathers.

That elephant, who had long drawn his bow against you, was honored by you with your six tusks—you who possess the luster of a mass of white, lofty, and massive clouds; even now, in the netherworld, he is worshipped by the serpents with their slackened hoods, as they offer him worship with their fangs, which are gruesome from the profuse blood spewed out when they tore open his temples.

Because you brought those men— whose boats were overturned by the lord of waters, whose waves were terrifying due to the tossing of the hoods of serpents in their fury, and which were churned by swarms of crocodiles—
to the edge of the shore by means of the great raft of your body out of love, all the worlds have been made your bride through that extraordinary deed of yours.

O King, just as you have fulfilled the hopes of your supplicants by crossing over the circular mountains and the lands girdled by ranges of water, and by obtaining the wish-fulfilling gem from within the interior of Badaradvīpa,
so too do the sprouts of the jewels of the true Dharma arise for the wise from you.

By that [practice], may there be for you the severance of the thirst for existence arising from birth— a yoga that restrains rebirth— since through it you brought about the appeasement of hunger with the flesh of demons whose dark bodies were like dense clouds spread as canopies, who robbed others of their vitality, and whose blood flowed from the openings of heads split by your sword-blades, while the flesh itself was not devoid of its natural warmth.

Because King Śibi, being virtuous, remained unattached even as a hawk—its throat parched and trembling with terror—scrambled upon his lap, he placed his own body upon the incomparable scale stained by the outpouring of the bird’s blood for the sake of its welfare; by that act, Māra was reduced to the insignificance of a tuft of fine silk upon a scale.

Since you cast aside even Lakṣmī—who grants desired fruits and is never-failing—and having made the lowest of births by forming connections with animal wombs, you brought relief through your own flesh to those agonizing pains that pierce the vital organs; therefore, the powers of your intellects, which cut through the poison of afflictions, remain unimpeded.

Having uprooted his two eyes—which were like a concentrated essence of beauty, like the fruit of the loftiness of meritorious powers, smeared with drops of blood, and appearing deep blue with the luster of shimmering water-lilies—you gave them to a Brahmin who was sightless; therefore, you have become the sole lofty lamp for this blind and dark world.

Thus, O Jina, this [work] composed for my own sake, adorned with the words of the Sages, has been presented; yet not even a fraction of the mass of your praises has been proclaimed by me. For, just as one drawing water from the ocean to fill the stars and the clouds might notice only a tiny drop of water on the shores at the edge of the tide, so too is my praise of you.

Through the merit arising from the composition of even a tiny fraction of the excellence of your conduct—a portion gathered by my devotion blooming with vast serenity—may I become a person solely intent on the vehicle of those who know all things and understand the welfare of others, one who is devoted to the supreme benefit of others and has little regard for their own self-interest. The *Jātakastava* by Ācārya Jñānayaśas.
